(i) homeostatic feedbacks between cyclins D and E and their cell cycle inhibitor, p27(Kipl), are critical for the control of cell growth and differentiation; (ii) the paradoxical increase of pRb seen in some cancers is associated with protection of the cells from growth inhibition; and (iii) cancer cells suffer from gene addiction and gene hypersensitivity disorders that might be exploitable in cancer chemopreventive and therapeutic interventions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of cell cycle control genes, and other genes involved in homeostatic feedback, in multistage human carcinogenesis.

the identification and characterization of genes that are involved in the multistage process, of carcinogenesis, and with the elucidation of the molecular basis of homeostasis in normal and cancer cells.
the molecular pathogenesis of human cancer, and the development of molecularly-targeted approaches for the prevention and treatment of human malignancies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the multistage process involves the acquisition of mutations and epigenetic alterations of genes that are involved in the regulation of cell cycle control, and other critical functions.
the multistage process is not a random, stochastic process.
cancer is an epigenetic disorder that involves the dysregulation of cell circuitry.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the cell cycle control genes are critical in multistage cancer development, that their expression is regulated by feedback loops involving homeostatic mechanisms, and that these feedback mechanisms are disrupted in cancer.
cancer cells have a 'gene addiction' to the cyclin D1 oncogene, and a paradoxical 'gene hypersensitivity disorder' to pRb.
the 'cancer cell' has a 'disordered circuitry'.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cell circuitry of cancer cells is often dysfunctional, and this dysfunction is likely to be a critical component of the multistage process that leads to the development of cancer.
the study of the molecular mechanisms of carcinogenesis is not only important for the basic understanding of the process but also for the development of rational cancer prevention and therapy.
the multistage process is not simply one of acquiring new functions, but of progressively losing old ones.
